examples.problem_statement: Examine the case of $\frac{1}{29}$: Begin with 1 (as usual) at the extreme right end and go on multiplying by 3 each time, “carrying over” the surplus digit or digits (if any) to the left (i.e. to be added to the next product to be determined). Thus, when we have obtained 14 digits i.e. ………………9 6 5 5 1 7 2 4 1 3 7 9 3 1, we find that we have reached 28; we know we have done half the work; and we get the first 14 digits by simply subtracting each of the above digits from NINE. ·0 3 4 4 8 2 7 5 8 6 2 0 6 8/

solution.description: Place a single 1 at the extreme right of the digit row. Every other digit of the expansion will be grown leftward from this seed, so nothing else is written yet.

Multiply the seed 1 by the working multiplier 3 (one more than the 2 standing in front of the 9 in 29). The product 3 is a single digit, so write it immediately to the left of the 1 and carry nothing.
Multiply the digit just written, 3, by 3 again. The product 9 still fits in one place, so record 9 to its left and once more there is nothing to carry.
Multiply the 9 by 3 to get 27. The product now needs two places, so only the units digit 7 joins the row and the tens digit 2 is carried into the next multiplication.
Multiply the newly written 7 by 3 and add the carried 2, giving 23. Write the 3 in the row and carry the 2 forward. This multiply-then-add-the-carry move is repeated for every remaining place.

Keep multiplying and carrying until fourteen digits stand in the row, reading 9 6 5 5 1 7 2 4 1 3 7 9 3 1. These are the last fourteen digits of the period, and the interim total 28 that has just been reached is the signal that exactly half the work is done.
Because 28 is one less than 29, the first half of the period is the nine's complement of the half already built. Subtract each of the fourteen digits from 9 instead of continuing to multiply.
Carrying out those fourteen subtractions produces the first half of the period: 0 3 4 4 8 2 7 5 8 6 2 0 6 8.
Write the first fourteen digits followed by the fourteen that were generated by multiplication to get the complete 28-digit repeating block for 1/29.

solution.description: Note that 49 is 7 times 7, so 1/49 is the familiar repeating decimal of 1/7, namely 0.142857..., divided once more by 7. Recognising this structure is what opens the shortcut.

solution.operation: Avoid direct long division (which would require 42 steps)
solution.description: Reject the obvious route first: dividing 1 by 49 the long way runs to 42 steps before the period closes, which is far too many to carry out mentally.

solution.operation: Apply Ekādhika method: multiply from right to left by 5 or divide from left to right by 5
solution.description: Apply the Ekadhika instead. Since 49 ends in 9, the working number is 5, and the digits can be produced either by multiplying right to left by 5 or by dividing left to right by 5.

solution.operation: After computing 21 digits, observe the remainder 48 (D ↔ N)
solution.description: Keep going until 21 digits are down, at which point the remainder 48 appears. Being one less than 49, that remainder marks the halfway point of the period.

solution.operation: Write the full 42-digit recurring decimal by combining the first 21 digits with their 9-complements
solution.description: Finish without any further division by writing the nine's complement of each of the first 21 digits after them, which completes the 42-digit repeating block.

examples.problem_statement: Analyze the successive remainders of the fraction 1/7.

solution.description: Set 1 divided by 7 out as a long division so that each successive remainder can be watched as well as each quotient digit; the quotient is known to repeat as 142857.
Bring down a zero to make 10. Seven goes into 10 once, so the first quotient digit is 1 and the remainder left over is 3.
Attach a zero to the remainder 3 to make 30. Seven goes into 30 four times, giving the quotient digit 4 and leaving remainder 2.
Attach a zero to the remainder 2 to make 20. Seven goes into 20 twice, giving the quotient digit 2 and leaving remainder 6.
Attach a zero to the remainder 6 to make 60. Seven goes into 60 eight times, giving the quotient digit 8 and leaving remainder 4.
Attach a zero to the remainder 4 to make 40. Seven goes into 40 five times, giving the quotient digit 5 and leaving remainder 5.

Attach a zero to the remainder 5 to make 50. Seven goes into 50 seven times, giving the quotient digit 7 and leaving remainder 1. That is the number the division started from, so the cycle closes here.
Read the remainders back in the order they appeared: 1, 3, 2, 6, 4, 5. There are six of them, matching the six-digit period of the decimal.

Pair the first remainder with the fourth, the second with the fifth and the third with the sixth. Each pair sums to 7, so the second half of the remainder cycle is the complement of the first half with respect to the divisor.

examples.answer: The remainders are: 1, 3, 2, 6, 4, 5. They are complementary pairs that sum to 7: (1,6), (3,4), (2,5).

concept.technique_name: Ekadhikena Purvena (By one more than the previous one) and cyclic number patterns

examples.problem_statement: In the case of $\frac{1}{17}$, the successive remainders are: $10, 15, 14, 4, 6, 9, 5, 16, 7, 2, 3, 13, 11, 8, 12, 1$. The last 8 remainders are complements from 17 of the first eight ones. Similarly, for $\frac{1}{19}$, the remainders are: $10, 15, 12, 6, 3, 11, 15, 17, 18, 9, 4, 7, 13, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1$, where the first nine remainders, when added successively to the next nine, give 19 each time. Using this pattern, find the recurring decimal equivalent of $\frac{2}{7}$ given that $\frac{1}{7} = 0.\overline{142857}$.

solution.description: Start from the single fact taken as known: the repeating block of 1/7 is 142857.
Since 2/7 is simply twice 1/7, its expansion can be reached by doubling that decimal rather than by dividing 2 by 7.
Double the repeating decimal digit by digit, carrying wherever a doubled digit passes 9. The string 142857142857... becomes 285714285714...
The same six digits 285714 recur without change, so the answer can be written compactly with a bar over that block.

Cross-check against the remainder cycle. Dividing 1 by 7 gives remainders 1, 3, 2, 6, 4, 5; doubling each of those and reducing by 7 gives 2, 6, 4, 5, 1, 3, the same six values started at a different place, which is exactly what the digits of 2/7 predict.
Notice that 285714 is not a new set of digits at all but the digits of 142857 read from a different starting point. This cyclic behaviour is what the remaining examples exploit.

examples.problem_statement: Find the recurring decimal equivalent for 2/7.

solution.description: Rank the six digits of the block 142857 by size: 1 is first, 2 second, 4 third, 5 fourth, 7 fifth and 8 sixth. The numerator 2 tells you to look for the digit ranked second.
The second-smallest digit is 2, so begin reading the cycle there and continue round in the fixed order 1-4-2-8-5-7, giving .285714.

examples.problem_statement: Find the recurring decimal equivalent for 3/7.

solution.description: Use the same size ranking of 1, 4, 2, 8, 5, 7. The numerator 3 points to the digit ranked third.
The third-smallest digit is 4, so the cycle is read from 4 onward in the same fixed order, giving .428571.

examples.problem_statement: Find the recurring decimal equivalent for 4/7.

solution.description: Rank the digits by size once more; the numerator 4 points to the digit ranked fourth.
The fourth-smallest digit is 5, so reading the cycle from 5 onward gives .571428.

solution.description: Divide 1 by 13 once to obtain the base block 076923. Every other thirteenth will be read off from this rather than divided out separately.
Double that block to get 153846. Its digits are not a rearrangement of 076923 read round, so a second independent cycle exists.
All twelve fractions from 1/13 to 12/13 draw on just these two six-digit cycles, 076923 and 153846, so no further division is needed.
List the first six thirteenths. Each one is one of the two cycles read from a different starting digit: 1/13, 3/13 and 4/13 come from 076923, while 2/13, 5/13 and 6/13 come from 153846.
List the remaining six the same way: 9/13, 10/13 and 12/13 are readings of 076923, while 7/13, 8/13 and 11/13 are readings of 153846.

Check the table by pairing fractions that add to 1. The blocks of 1/13 and 12/13, 076923 and 923076, add digit for digit to 999999, so the two decimals sum to exactly 1.0 and the listing is consistent.

solution.operation: Observe that the dividend becomes 28, which is less than 49 (D < N).
solution.description: The next dividend formed is 28, which is smaller than the denominator 49. That is the signal that half of the period has been produced and the division need not be pushed further.

solution.operation: Write the last three quotient digits as complements from nine: 5, 7, 1.
solution.description: Write the three remaining digits as complements from nine of the three already found: 9 minus 4 is 5, 9 minus 2 is 7, 9 minus 8 is 1, giving 5, 7 and 1.

solution.operation: Alternatively, continue division until dividend becomes 21 (starting point), confirming recurrence.
